Drunken
DRUNK-en
adj., v. (pp.)
Older past participle of drink, used adjectivally. Webster 1828: intoxicated; inebriated; also, saturated with liquor. In the Authorized Version it names a literal sin, a figure for staggering judgment, and, in Revelation, the condition of a persecuting power drunk with the blood of the saints.

Biblical Definition

The first man in Scripture called drunken is the man who came through the flood: he drank of the wine, and was drunken; and he was uncovered within his tent (Genesis 9:21). Scripture reports the sin of its heroes without softening. Eli misjudges Hannah at prayer — Eli thought she had been drunken (1 Samuel 1:13) — a warning to every pastor about reading a grieving woman’s silence. Then the figure. The wicked and the judged reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end (Psalm 107:27). Isaiah sees a Jerusalem drunken, but not with wine (Isaiah 51:21), staggering under the cup of God’s fury, and a Judah drunken, but not with wine under a spirit of deep sleep (Isaiah 29:9). At Pentecost the charge is answered plainly: these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day (Acts 2:15). Paul rebukes a church whose Supper had become a meal where one is hungry, and another is drunken (1 Corinthians 11:21). And John sees the great harlot drunken with the blood of the saints (Revelation 17:6), the last and most terrible use: a power intoxicated by persecution.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DRUNKEN as intoxicated; inebriated; and, figuratively, saturated or overpowered. The KJV keeps both the literal sin and the figure of a man who cannot stand.

expand to see more

DRUNKEN, a. — Intoxicated; inebriated with strong liquor.

Given to habitual excessive drinking; as, a drunken man.

Saturated with liquor or moisture; drenched.

The figurative force in Scripture is Webster’s third sense combined with the first: a man saturated by something until he can no longer stand upright, whether the cup is wine or the wrath of God.

Key Scripture

Genesis 9:21 — "And he drank of the wine, and was drunken; and he was uncovered within his tent."

1 Samuel 1:13 — "Now Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken."

Psalm 107:27 — "They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end."

Acts 2:15 — "For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day."

Revelation 17:6 — "And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus: and when I saw her, I wondered with great admiration."

Modern Corruption

Drunkenness is corrupted in two directions: by a culture that treats it as recreation rather than as a sin Scripture excludes men from the kingdom for, and by a false piety that forbids what God permits and so loses the authority to forbid what He prohibits.

expand to see more

Scripture is not silent or ambiguous. Drunkenness stands in the lists that end shall not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:10; Galatians 5:21), and Paul commands, be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). The contemporary treatment of intoxication as harmless leisure, and of habitual drunkenness as a condition with no moral dimension at all, cannot be squared with those texts. Scripture does speak of the drunkard with pity and warns of the misery in Proverbs 23, and pastoral care is right to reckon with the ruin it causes in body and household — but it names the thing sin, and it calls for repentance and not merely management.

The opposite error is common in reaction. The Bible blesses wine as God’s gift to make glad the heart of man (Psalm 104:15), our Lord made it at Cana, and Paul counselled Timothy to use a little for his stomach. A church that forbids what Scripture permits has stepped outside its authority, and it will find that its warnings against what Scripture forbids carry less weight for having done so. The line is drawn where Scripture draws it: not at the cup, but at the loss of self-command that Genesis 9:21 records of Noah and 1 Corinthians 11:21 records of the Corinthians at the Lord’s table.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew shakar means to become drunk or satiated; the Greek methuo is the ordinary word for intoxication, used literally at Pentecost and figuratively of the harlot in Revelation.

expand to see more

Hebrew shakar (H7937) — to be or become drunk, to be satiated; he drank of the wine, and was drunken (Genesis 9:21).

Hebrew shikkor (H7910) — a drunkard, one intoxicated; the figure in Psalm 107:27 and Isaiah 19:14.

Greek methuo (G3184) — to be drunk; these are not drunken (Acts 2:15), another is drunken (1 Corinthians 11:21), the woman drunken with the blood of the saints (Revelation 17:6).

Greek methe (G3178) — drunkenness, listed among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:21).

The KJV distinguishes drunken as participle-adjective from drunkard as a settled character; the second is the term of the vice lists.

Usage

"He drank of the wine, and was drunken (Genesis 9:21) — the sin of a righteous man reported without softening."

"Eli thought she had been drunken (1 Samuel 1:13) — a priest misjudging a woman’s silent prayer."

"The woman drunken with the blood of the saints (Revelation 17:6) — persecution as intoxication."
